opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, especially working in robot learning, where the field has swung between a lot of different bets over the years.

For me, it comes down to a few things. The first is whether there's a plausible path to scale. When I look at a direction, I ask: if this works a little bit today, is there a reason to believe it will work a lot better with more data, more compute, or more engineering effort? Or does it hit a wall that is fundamental? A lot of methods look great on a carefully chosen benchmark but don't have a story for how they get better over time. The ones I get excited about have some kind of flywheel.

The second is whether it addresses a real bottleneck rather than a convenient one. In robotics, it's very easy to work on problems that are tractable in simulation or on a specific setup but aren't actually what's stopping robots from being useful in the real world. So I try to be honest about what the real bottleneck is. For a long time, I think that was data: how do you get enough diverse, high-quality robot experience? That's part of why I've cared so much about things like imitation learning, data collection systems, and learning from human demonstrations. Directions that attack the true constraint tend to pay off, even if they're less glamorous.

Third, I pay attention to early signals that are surprising in the right way. Sometimes you run an experiment and something works better than it has any right to, like generalizing to a situation you didn't train on. That kind of surprise is often a hint that there's something deeper there. On the flip side, if a direction only works when everything is tuned just right, that's a warning sign.

And finally, there's a personal element. I ask myself whether I'd still want to work on this even if it takes five years and the field moves on to something trendier. Research is a long game, and conviction matters. You need to believe in it enough to push through the phase where nothing works. But I also try to hold that belief loosely enough that I can update when the evidence says I'm wrong. It's a balance between conviction and humility, and I don't think anyone gets it right all the time. You just try to make good bets and learn from the ones that don't pan out.

r001.rationale: The response presents scalability and surprising experimental results as separate considerations, but it does not identify first-principles reasoning that a direction is inevitable as one of the grounds.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've gone back and forth on a lot, honestly, because I don't think there's a clean formula. But I can tell you the heuristics I actually use.

The first one is almost embarrassingly simple: does the direction have a path to scaling? Not scaling in the narrow sense of "throw more GPUs at it," but in the sense of whether progress compounds. If I imagine the field putting two or three more years of effort into this, does it get meaningfully better, or does it plateau? A lot of ideas in robotics have looked beautiful in a single demo and then just... stopped. They had no gradient to follow. When I was working on task planning and representation learning earlier in my career, the thing that eventually pulled me toward data-driven approaches was exactly that — I could see that hand-designed structure gave you a nice result today but nowhere to go tomorrow.

The second thing I look for is whether the direction is anchored in something real about the problem rather than something real about our current tools. There's a tendency to pick directions because they fit the methods we happen to have — "we're good at this kind of model, so let's find a problem that fits it." That can work, but it's fragile. I try to ask: if the tools changed completely, would this still be the right question? For robot learning, the bottleneck is clearly data and the gap between what's demonstrable in the lab and what works in an open-ended environment. Directions that attack that gap directly feel more durable to me than ones that attack an artifact of today's architectures.

The third one is more personal and harder to defend rigorously, which is: can I articulate why it would fail? If I can't name a concrete failure mode, I'm probably not understanding the direction well enough to believe in it. Good directions have visible risks. When I talk to students about a project, I'll often ask them to tell me the version of the story where this doesn't work, and if they can do that convincingly and still want to pursue it, that's a strong signal. Belief without a model of failure is just enthusiasm.

And then I'd add a caveat that I think people underweight: you don't have to decide once. I treat belief in a direction as something I update continuously, and I try to set up early experiments specifically to produce evidence that would change my mind. The worst outcome isn't betting on the wrong thing — it's betting on the wrong thing and building a research program that's incapable of noticing. So I'd say I believe in a direction when it has room to compound, when it's about the problem and not the tool, when I can see how it breaks, and when I've designed a way to find out quickly if I'm wrong.

r001.rationale: The response offers several heuristics, including whether progress can compound and whether early experiments could change the speaker’s mind. It does not distinguish first-principles reasoning that a direction is inevitable from observed early signs of viability as two grounds for belief.

astra-6.text:
For me, it starts with asking: if this works, what would it actually enable? Would it remove a fundamental bottleneck, or would it just make something we already do a little better? I’m more willing to invest in a direction when I can see a meaningful capability on the other side.

Then I ask what evidence would make me believe it. You don’t need to solve the whole problem immediately, but you should be able to design a small experiment that tests the central assumption. And you have to be willing to update your view when that experiment doesn’t go the way you hoped.

So I think it’s a combination of a long-term vision and a short-term feedback loop. The vision gives you a reason to persist; the experiments help you decide whether that persistence is justified.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long-term vision and experimental feedback, but it does not distinguish first-principles reasoning that a direction is inevitable from observed early signs of viability.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it starts with asking: if this works, what would it enable? Is it addressing a fundamental bottleneck, or just improving something we already know how to do? I don’t need to see the entire path to a solution, but I do want a concrete reason to believe the core idea could work.

Then I look for small experiments that can challenge that belief. What’s the simplest setting where we should see a benefit? And what result would make us reconsider? A positive result is much more convincing when you’ve given the idea a real chance to fail.

So I think it’s a combination of a compelling long-term question and evidence you can gather in the short term. You need enough conviction to stay with a difficult problem, but enough flexibility to change your approach.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a compelling long-term question with short-term experimental evidence, but it does not communicate that first-principles reasoning about a direction’s inevitability is distinct from observed early signs of viability.
